exact: 3PL stands for third-party logistics. It means a business hires an outside company to handle part or all its supply chain operations, such as warehousing, inventory tracking, packing, shipping, and returns.
simple: Another firm does logistics work for you.
example: Campus Tees pays a firm to store, pack and send shirts.
note: The agreement decides which tasks it does.

exact:
Fourth-party logistics (4PL) is a supply chain management model where a company outsources its entire end-to-end logistics network and strategy to a single external provider.

4PL has a high-level management focus, handling integration and oversight of the entire supply chain often including a 3PL.
simple: One firm plans and manages a wider logistics network.
example: Campus Tees uses a partner to coordinate storage firms and carriers.
note: The key role is coordination, not just transport.

exact:
A common way to classify inventory is the ABC classification.

A items have a high value, often representing about 80% of the total inventory

B items have medium value

C items have low value

ABC classification is used to put effort to items that affect the result the most. It is connected to the Pareto criteria (80/20 rule) where 20% of you inventory items represent 80% of the cost.
simple: Spend more time managing items with high annual usage value.
example: Campus Tees checks its high-value blank-shirt stock often.
note: A cheap item can still stop work if it is missing.

exact: Agile supply chain management focuses on flexibility and responsiveness to meet rapidly changing customer demands and market conditions. It also makes the process efficient and empowers the employees.
simple: Respond to changing demand with good information and flexible work.
example: Campus Tees changes the print mix after clubs confirm their designs.
note: Speed must still meet cost and quality needs.

exact: Business Process Reengineering (BPR) is the radical redesign of core business workflows and processes to achieve dramatic improvements in productivity, cycle times, and quality
simple: Make a major change to a business process.
example: Campus Tees replaces separate order forms with one shared order flow.
note: Kaizen usually means smaller, ongoing improvements.

exact: The Economic Order Quantity is the optimal number of items to order at a given time. The EOQ formula (sometime referred to as the Wilson formula) balances two costs. The cost of ordering inventory falls with the increase in ordering volume due to purchasing on economies of scale. However, as the size of inventory grows, the cost of holding the inventory rises. EOQ is the exact point that minimizes both of these inversely related costs, see appendix A for the formula and its variables.
simple: Find the order size that balances ordering and holding costs.
example: For D=12,000, K=€30 and h=€2, Campus Tees orders 600 blanks.
note: The basic model assumes steady demand and a fixed unit price.

exact: Enterprise resource planning (ERP) is the integrated management of main business processes, often in real time and mediated by software and technology.
simple: Join data and processes across the business.
example: Campus Tees links sales, purchasing and finance.
note: The data must still be correct.

exact: Just-in-time (JIT) inventory management aims to increase efficiency and reduce costs by ordering products only on an as-needed basis.
simple: Bring materials close to the time they are needed.
example: Campus Tees gets reliable small deliveries of packing material.
note: JIT needs reliable quality, information and suppliers.

exact: Kanban is a just-in-time system in which new item orders are triggered automatically via cards or other signals.
simple: Use a signal to tell someone to refill used stock.
example: An empty box tells the supplier to send more blanks.
note: Set a suitable amount and refill time.

exact: Kaizen is a Japanese philosophy focusing on continuous improvement.
simple: Keep making small improvements.
example: Campus Tees improves its artwork checklist after an error.
note: Check whether the change helps.

exact: The oldest items in the inventory are sold first. Therefore, the cost of the oldest item should be used when calculating your cost of sold goods. Compare with LIFO.
simple: Use the oldest inventory cost first.
example: Buy ten blanks at €2, then ten at €3. FIFO cost for ten sold is €20.
note: The accounting rule and physical stock movement can differ.

exact: Lean supply chain management focuses on waste reduction, inventory optimization and continuous improvement,
simple: Remove waste and keep work flowing.
example: Campus Tees removes duplicate order entry and waiting.
note: Do not remove a useful buffer without checking the effect.

exact: When using LIFO as an inventory valuation method it is assumed that the Last items in are sold First. An example of this could be companies that sell sand or gravel. Compare with FIFO.
simple: Use the newest inventory cost first.
example: Buy ten blanks at €2, then ten at €3. LIFO cost for ten sold is €30.
note: This explains the idea, not where accounting rules allow it.

exact: A production plan that helps you to determine when to order and how to allocate production resources like personnel and machines.
simple: Plan the finished output and its timing.
example: Campus Tees plans to print 300 shirts next week.
note: MRP then plans the materials needed.

exact: MRO items are anything that is used to maintain, repair, and operate your inventory management system.
simple: Supplies used to keep the business running.
example: Campus Tees buys cleaning fluid and printer spares.
note: These support the work rather than form the main product.

exact: Material Requirements Planning is a system that helps businesses manage inventory by determining what materials are needed, in what quantities, and when they are required for production.
simple: Plan the materials, amounts and timing needed for output.
example: A plan for 300 shirts uses stock data to find how many blanks to buy.
note: Also check planned deliveries and lead times.

exact: There are seven kinds of waste (MUDA), 1 Overproduction, 2 Defects, 3 Inventory, 4 Motion, 5 Over processing, 6 Transporting, 7 Waiting.
simple: Find seven types of waste.
example: Campus Tees finds waiting, wrong prints and extra box movements.
note: Motion is people moving; transport is goods moving.

exact: Quick Response (QR) Code Inventory Management uses scannable optical labels to track stock levels, locations, and product details in real time.
simple: The source paragraph explains scanning QR codes to identify stock.
example: Campus Tees scans a box when it arrives.
note: The glossary heading uses QR differently from an agile quick-response strategy.

exact: Radio-frequency identification (RFID) is used in inventory management to track individual items within the system.
simple: Use radio tags to identify or track items.
example: Campus Tees reads tagged shirt boxes at the warehouse.
note: The recorded movement must still be correct.

exact: A safety stock (often referred to as a buffer stock) is extra inventory held to protect against stockouts caused by demand fluctuations or supply delays.
simple: Keep extra stock against late supply or higher demand.
example: Campus Tees holds 60 extra blank shirts.
note: The amount depends on service needs and uncertainty.

exact: Six Sigma is a data-driven methodology and set of techniques used to improve business processes by eliminating defects and reducing variability
simple: Use data to reduce defects and variation.
example: Campus Tees measures wrong prints and checks their causes.
note: Measure the result of each change.

exact: A stock-keeping unit (SKU) is a code attached to items within your inventory often in form of a barcode, QR code or RFID tags.
simple: Give each separately managed stock variant an ID.
example: Small white and medium white shirts have different SKUs.
note: Barcodes, QR codes and RFID can carry this ID.

exact: An organisation-wide effort to work with quality and continous improvement (Kaizen). Today often replaced by ISO9000, Six Sigma and Lean manufacturing.
simple: Make quality a responsibility across the whole business.
example: Sales and printing work together to prevent wrong logos.
note: TQM, lean and Six Sigma can be used together.

exact: Vendor-managed inventory (VMI) is inventory that is monitored and replenished by the vendor itself—rather than the business owner.
simple: The supplier checks stock and refills it under agreed rules.
example: The packing supplier checks use and refills Campus Tees’ boxes.
note: VMI does not by itself decide who owns the stock.

exact: A WMS helps a business to manage day-to-day operations within their warehouse.
simple: Manage daily warehouse tasks and stock locations.
example: Campus Tees uses a WMS to receive, find, pick and send shirts.
note: ERP joins wider business data; MRP plans materials.
